how-the-pieces-move.p: Chess is played on 64 squares by two armies of sixteen pieces. Set the board so that each player has a light square in the bottom right corner, and put the queen on her own colour: the white queen on a light square, the black queen on a dark one.

castling.t: Castling: the rule and when to use it
castling.p: Castling is the only move where two pieces move at once. The king slides two squares towards a rook, and that rook jumps to the square the king crossed. Short castling goes towards the h-file, long castling towards the a-file.

en-passant.t: En passant, the rule everyone forgets
en-passant.p: When a pawn advances two squares from its starting rank and lands beside an enemy pawn, that enemy pawn may capture it as if it had only moved one square. The capture happens on the square the pawn skipped over.

pawn-promotion.t: Pawn promotion and the underpromotion trick
pawn-promotion.p: A pawn reaching the far rank must immediately become a queen, rook, bishop or knight of its own colour. It is not a choice between promoting and staying a pawn: the change is compulsory.

check-checkmate-stalemate.p: A king is in check when an enemy piece attacks his square. You must answer a check at once, in one of three ways: move the king, capture the attacker, or block the line between them. A knight check can never be blocked, which is what makes knights so dangerous near a king.

how-games-are-drawn.t: Every way a chess game can be drawn
how-games-are-drawn.p: A draw is not a failure, it is a result, and there are five routes to it. Stalemate: the side to move has no legal move and is not in check. Agreement: both players simply accept a draw.

chess-notation.p: Every square has a name: files a to h from White's left, ranks 1 to 8 from White's side. The bottom-left square is a1, the top-right is h8.

time-controls.t: Time controls: what blitz, rapid and 10+0 mean
time-controls.p: Every timed game is written as two numbers: the minutes each side starts with, and the seconds given back after every move, the increment. 10+0 means ten minutes and no increment; 3+2 means three minutes plus two extra seconds on every move you make.

opening-principles.t: The four opening principles that matter
opening-principles.p: You do not need opening theory to play a decent opening. Four ideas cover almost everything.

spotting-a-hanging-piece.p: A piece is hanging when it can be captured for free: nothing defends it, or what defends it is worth less than the attacker risks. Most tactics below build on top of this one skill, so it comes first.

knight-fork.p: A fork is one piece attacking two targets at once, so the opponent can only save one of them. The knight is the classic forking piece: its L-shaped move lets it attack squares that look completely unrelated to each other from anywhere else on the board.

pawn-fork.p: Pawns capture diagonally, one square forward. That single detail means a single pawn already attacks two squares at once, which makes it a natural forking piece the moment two enemy pieces line up on those two diagonals.

double-attack.t: Double attack: forks that aren't knight moves
double-attack.p: Any piece can create a fork, not only knights and pawns. A queen, rook or bishop attacking two targets at once from a single square works on exactly the same logic: the opponent has one move to save two things.

the-pin.t: The pin: a piece that can't move
the-pin.p: A piece is pinned when moving it would expose a more valuable piece behind it, usually the king, to attack. A pinned piece is not captured or threatened directly: it is simply frozen, unable to do its normal job.

the-skewer.t: The skewer: a pin turned around
the-skewer.p: A skewer is a pin in reverse. Instead of a low-value piece shielding a high-value one, the high-value piece is in front and forced to move, uncovering something less valuable directly behind it on the same line.

back-rank-mate.p: Castling tucks the king away safely, and the pawns in front of it feel like protection. They can just as easily become a wall with the king inside it: a king with no pawn moved in front of it has nowhere to go if a rook or queen reaches its back rank.

deflection.p: Some pieces end up doing two jobs at once without anyone intending it: a queen defending a piece on one line while also being the only thing stopping a checkmate on another. Deflection is attacking that piece to force it to choose.

the-quiet-move.t: The quiet move: the hardest kind to find
the-quiet-move.p: Every pattern above starts the same way: a capture or a check, something forcing and loud. A quiet move does neither. It doesn't take anything and doesn't give check, which is exactly why it's the hardest kind of winning move to find.

your-account.t: Your chang64 account: free, optional, a username and a code
your-account.p: chang64 works without an account, and it will stay that way. An account first brings this: your progress follows you. Your puzzle rating, your badges, your day streak, your preferences and your games are also saved on our server, so you find them again on your phone, your tablet and your computer, and you keep them if you clear your browser or change device.

fork.p: One piece attacks two or more enemy pieces at the same time. Knights are the classic forkers because their move cannot be blocked, and a fork hitting the king and the queen wins material outright.

pin.p: A piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it. If the piece behind is the king, the pin is absolute and the pinned piece is legally frozen.

hanging-piece.p: A piece that is attacked and not defended. Scanning for hanging pieces before every move eliminates most blunders at club level.

blunder.p: A move that loses material or the game outright, usually because a threat or a hanging piece was missed. Most of chang64's tactics puzzles exist because a real player, somewhere, made exactly this mistake.

mistake.p: A move that makes the position clearly worse without losing outright, one notch below a blunder. It hands the opponent a real advantage rather than an immediate win.

inaccuracy.p: A move that is not the best available and quietly gives something back: a tempo, a square, a fraction of an advantage. Rarely punished on the spot, but a habit of inaccuracies is how good positions slip away.

elo-rating.t: The Elo rating: what your number means
elo-rating.p: An Elo rating is a running estimate of skill built from one simple idea: each result nudges the number up or down by an amount that depends on how surprising it was. Beating someone much stronger moves it a lot; beating someone much weaker barely moves it at all. chang64 treats each puzzle level as an opponent of a fixed strength and updates your rating the same way after every attempt. Worth saying plainly: this number is a personal, relative tracker, not a certified skill measurement. Sites like Lichess calibrate their puzzle ratings against millions of real attempts from real players, cross-checked against each other; chang64 keeps no accounts and tracks nothing across players, by design, so there is no population to calibrate against. Your rating here is honest about your own progress over time. It isn't a claim that a given number equals the same strength on Lichess or in a FIDE-rated tournament. That doesn't make it meaningless: watching it rise still means exactly what it always has, that you're solving problems that used to be out of reach.

stalemate.p: The player to move has no legal move and is not in check. The game is an immediate draw, which makes stalemate the standard escape when losing: trap the enemy king with no checks and no moves left, and a lost position survives.

fifty-move-rule.p: Either player can claim a draw if 50 moves pass, by both sides, without a pawn move or a capture. It exists to stop a player with no real winning method from shuffling pieces forever hoping for a mistake.

threefold-repetition.p: A draw can be claimed if the same position, with the same player to move, occurs three times in a game. It's the usual way a perpetual check is actually recorded as a result, rather than checking forever.
